summary:
Louisiana stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed these restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and the American Civil Liberties Union's suit on behalf of seven plaintiffs remains in federal court. By March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries separate exposure. Since 25 February 2025 the State Department has flagged visa applicants with an internal marking, treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth, in the context of barring trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports. Separately, Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Louisiana records the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state in the country: 24.7 per 100,000 people per year reported, on 19 recorded victims, against 23.5 for the state ranked safest. The count rests on a base of 428 victims recorded across the United States between 2008 and 2025, and every figure in that base is an undercount floor. A national analysis drawing on that data cautions that rankings built on legal risk do not sort physical safety: the states holding the worst law carry the highest rate.

Violence in Louisiana has also produced prosecutions of the people attacked. In August 2026 a mob beat trans couple Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders over restroom use at Cypress Black Bayou Park in Benton. Sanders, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and Rush, who suffered a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested, and the Sheriff's Office reported no other arrests that day. Rush was denied hospital care, jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence. The plea deal offered to the victims was not signed.

The same municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances, placing local restroom access for trans residents and visitors on a restrictive footing at the time of the attack.

Custody is a documented site of harm. On 2 April 2024 Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates. She was at least the 16th trans or gender-expansive person killed that year and the fifth in April alone, and such deaths are systematically under- or mis-reported.
tangentialFactors:
A national analysis published in July 2026 argues that legal-risk rankings and physical-safety outcomes diverge: the state with the strictest law does not hold the worst killing rate, and the states with the worst law hold the highest. A trans visitor reading a legal index alone would therefore misjudge Louisiana in both directions.

The underlying dataset of 428 victims recorded nationally between 2008 and 2025 is described by its compilers as an undercount floor, and memorial reporting notes that deaths of trans and gender-expansive people are systematically under- or mis-reported, so all Louisiana figures should be read as minimums.

Facilities law remains patchwork nationally: state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory, while 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Louisiana's own position in that count is not established by the sources assembled here.

Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and federal measures including Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025, the military purge under Executive Order 14183 and the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201 are in force or in litigation. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.
localsOnly:
Local restroom restrictions and enforcement fall hardest on residents using public facilities daily. In Benton the attacked couple were the parties charged, and the municipality voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances in the same period, which binds local users rather than visitors alone.

Jail classification does not follow state identity documents. Aurora Rush was held in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her Louisiana driver's licence, and she was denied hospital care before intake.

Trans people held in the state prison system face lethal risk: Yella (Robert) Clark Jr. was killed at Angola on 2 April 2024 while serving a life sentence, one of at least 16 trans or gender-expansive people killed nationally in 2024.

The Louisiana driver's licence 'female' marker in Rush's case indicates that some form of state-issued marker change was available to her, but the inventory does not establish the procedure, the evidence required, or whether it remains open.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Louisiana permits change of gender marker on a birth certificate or driver's licence, and on what evidence, is unresolved: no source in the inventory states the Louisiana rule, though one account shows a licence carrying a 'female' marker.

Whether Louisiana's hate-crime statute covers offences motivated by anti-trans bias, and whether prosecutors have used it, is not sourced here.

Whether Louisiana has a statewide ban on trans people's use of sex-segregated facilities is not established by the inventory; the only Louisiana facility restriction documented is the municipal ordinance adopted in Benton. Its current status, and whether it has been challenged, are unresolved.

The plea deal offered to Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders was reported unsigned at the time of reporting in August 2026; whether the disturbing-the-peace charges were later dropped, reduced or prosecuted is unresolved.

The stated comparison of 24.7 per 100,000 per year for Louisiana against 23.5 for the state ranked safest comes from a single national analysis and is reproduced as reported; the underlying methodology behind the near-parity of those two figures is not resolved in the inventory.
